catalog_quote: Hiligaynon has twenty-five significant sounds plus accent. ... Accented words have one primary stress. Some words have no stress of their own but rather "lean" on words which do. Stressless words are referred to as clitics or particles. A cluster of a stressed word together with one or more particles is a stress group. ... 1.2. Accent and Intonation. The term accent here refers to the emphasizing of a syllable in a word by means of loudness, vowel length, pitch, or a combination of these. Some words may have more than one accented syllable. All words except the grammatical particles have one primary accented syllable and if more than two syllables usually a secondary accent on one of the other syllables. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Hiligaynon has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this fills rather than agrees or contradicts: it establishes that accent is lexically contrastive (compatible with the penult-vs-final contrast reported by Zorc 2001, Motus 1971 and Wolfenden 1971, all read in the earlier reading or this one), but it gives no placement and stresses local variation. Identical paragraph to Lozano 1876 §12.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (realized as vowel length/quantity) distinguishes word meaning, but the author declines to give a rule for it because its placement/quantity differs from town to town; no default position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialectal: the same word is pronounced 'long' in some towns and 'short' in others, which is why the author refuses to codify accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Lozano's 'lengua panayana' / 'visaya-panayana' is the 19th-century Bisayan of Panay island, i.e. the Hiligaynon (Ilonggo) area; the MPG PuRe subject tags (ceb Cebuano + hil for the 1892 item; bsd 'Bisaya, Sarawak' for the 1876 item) are cataloguing artefacts, not the content. Lozano explicitly notes town-by-town variation in accent (length) within Panay. Wolfenden 1971 (supplementary) describes the standard Iloilo Hiligaynon of the Peace Corps course.

Wolfenden 1975 (index 0) was re-probed (SIL 404, archive.org 403, archive.org search-inside 403 for 'stress' and 'accent') and remains unreadable. audit.recode_to: kind stays 'lexical'. Optional refinement from Zorc 1977 sec. 3.1.3/10.2.1 and Zorc 2001 p. 301: accent window = final two syllables (penult or ultima); words with a closed penult (CVC.CV(C)) take penult accent predictably, so the lexical contrast is confined to open-penult words; accented open penult realised as vowel length. This would replace the the primary-stress rule sentence 'No positional or weight-based rule is stated' and could populate the edge/weight fields.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the djvu text we hold of Wolfenden 1971 at the stated places (sec. 1 p. 10; sec. 1.2 pp. 24-25) and the page image we hold of printed p. 25 shows the minimal pairs with accents. (2) Deciding source is a 238-pp linguist's reference grammar (1971), the standard description of the language; Glottolog lists no phonology monograph, no JIPA Illustration exists (checked), and Crossref shows no stress/prosody study. The two specialist sources by Zorc (1977 comparative Bisayan monograph. 2001 encyclopedia sketch, downloaded now) and Motus 1971 (downloaded now) all independently state that accent is lexically contrastive, so the lexical coding is secure. (3) Zorc adds two facts Wolfenden does not state: accent is limited to the last two syllables, and closed-penult words are predictably penult-accented; these refine, not contradict

sources.quote: 'Stress is important in Hiligaynon in that it makes for a difference in meaning in some instances ... One syllable is pronounced louder than the other or others. This prominence is called stress. Example: punu' means 'tree trunk, leader, etc.' while punu' [other accent] means 'full to capacity'.' Drill lists accent pairs laba/laba', punu'/punu', bulag/bulag, pilak/pilak. (Same statement in Motus 1971 Hiligaynon Dictionary intro sec. III, fetched as : 'Stress is phonemic in Hiligaynon'.)

sources.quote: 'Word accent is very important in distinguishing forms in Hiligaynon. Roots generally have accent on either the second last or final syllable, as in: ámo 'master' (Sp.) vs. amó 'the same, thus', áyaw ... vs. ayáw ..., bála vs. balá, báti vs. batí, bílin vs. bilín, dúlot vs. dulút, súbong vs. subóng, and útud vs. utúd. If the accent falls on the second last syllable (penult) and that syllable is not closed by a consonant ... the vowel is pronounced long ... If the accent falls on the final syllable, then that syllable receives stress (is pronounced louder and with a slight change in pitch), whi
sources.note: Most recent specialist statement: accent falls on penult or final (two-syllable window), eight minimal pairs, phonetic realisation (length on open penult, stress+pitch on final); a second independent citation for the lexical coding.
